items.question: We already track FID in our dashboard, so our responsiveness story is covered, right?
items.answer: No. FID was replaced by INP as the responsiveness Core Web Vital (https://web.dev/articles/inp). FID only observed the input delay of the first interaction on the page, while INP observes the full duration of click, tap, and keyboard interactions, from the interaction until the next frame can be presented, across the whole page lifetime. A dashboard can show a healthy FID while real users suffer slow interactions that FID never measured.
items.trap: FID and INP sound like the same 'input responsiveness' metric, and legacy dashboards still display FID, so the naive answer assumes they are interchangeable. FID's blind spots (only the first interaction, only the input-delay portion) are exactly what INP was designed to cover.

items.question: Our median LCP is 1.9 seconds, so we pass the LCP assessment, right?
items.answer: Not necessarily. The Core Web Vitals assessment uses field distributions at the 75th percentile, segmented by mobile and desktop (https://web.dev/articles/vitals). A good median can coexist with a heavy tail: if enough loads are slower than the 'good' threshold, the p75 fails even though the median looks healthy. Report the distribution and check the p75 per segment.
items.trap: The median feels like 'the typical user', so it reads as a pass. The standard is the 75th percentile, which deliberately weighs the tail; a median can hide the exact population that fails.

items.question: We compressed the hero image by 60% and field LCP did not move. Why?
items.answer: Because image bytes only affect one of the four LCP sub-parts: resource-load duration. LCP time is the sum of TTFB, resource-load delay, resource-load duration, and render delay (https://web.dev/articles/lcp). If the dominant phase is slow TTFB, late discovery of the resource, or render delay (for example client-side rendering or hydration), compressing the image changes nothing. Identify the LCP element and split the timeline into the four phases first, then fix the largest one.
items.trap: The naive mental model is 'LCP equals image weight', so the fix is always compression. When the bottleneck is a different phase, the image fix is invisible in the metric and the team concludes that performance work does not pay off.

items.question: The LCP element turned out to be a text block, not the hero image. What changes about the fix?
items.answer: The image playbook stops applying. For a text LCP element, look at TTFB and render delay: render-blocking CSS, whether the text is server-rendered versus rendered or hydrated on the client, and font loading if the font swap changes what renders. The investigation still follows the same four phases, but the fixes move to server timing, CSS delivery, and rendering strategy.
items.trap: Teams assume the LCP element is the hero image and ship image optimizations on autopilot. The metric follows whatever element is actually largest in the viewport, so optimizing the wrong element produces zero metric movement.

items.question: Lighthouse shows green Total Blocking Time, so INP must be fine. Right?
items.answer: No. TBT is a lab metric that sums main-thread blocking during the scripted load; it never observes a real interaction. Field INP can be poor even with green TBT because real users interact after load, on real devices, with handlers and layout work the lab run never triggers. TBT is a useful lab diagnostic for load-time blocking, but it is not a replacement for field INP (https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp).
items.trap: Both metrics are about 'the main thread being busy', so green TBT reads as proof of good responsiveness. One is a synthetic load-time proxy; the other measures the latency of actual interactions from real pageviews.

items.question: We made the click handler cheaper by debouncing it, and INP got worse. Why?
items.answer: INP measures from the interaction until the next frame is presented. Debounce delays the first visual response, which is exactly the portion of the interaction the metric observes. The pattern that works is to give immediate, small visual feedback (for example a pending state on the next frame) and defer only the work that does not need to block that feedback.
items.trap: The instinct is 'slow handler means delay the handler'. But INP is not measuring handler CPU cost in isolation; it measures time to the next presented frame, so postponing feedback adds latency to the very number you are trying to improve.

items.question: The only layout shift on the page happens right after the user taps a button. Does it count against CLS?
items.answer: Possibly not. Shifts that occur close to a discrete user input like a tap, click, or key press can be excluded by the metric's rules; the layout-shift entry carries a hadRecentInput flag that marks these (https://web.dev/articles/cls). But the exclusion is narrow and defined: it does not cancel shifts from network responses, ads, or late fonts that happen to land after a click. Check the actual layout-shift entries rather than assuming, and do not use the exclusion as a reason to leave unrelated shifts unaddressed.
items.trap: People answer in absolutes: 'user-triggered shifts never count' or 'every shift counts'. The metric has a specific, bounded exclusion around discrete inputs, and shifts outside it, or caused by something else that coincidentally follows an input, still count.

items.question: Lighthouse reports CLS 0 for the page, but support tickets say it jumps all over the place. How can both be true?
items.answer: A lab run loads the page once with scripted behavior and usually misses shifts that happen after the initial load: content injected on scroll, late embeds and ads, font swaps after interaction. Record layout-shift entries or use DevTools while performing the real user flow, and verify CLS in field data, because lab loading usually misses shifts that happen later in the page lifecycle (https://web.dev/articles/lab-and-field-data-differences).
items.trap: A clean lab CLS reads as proof of stability. The lab scenario defines what was measured; if the shifting content appears after scroll or seconds later, the lab never saw it, so the 0 is an artifact of the scenario, not evidence.

items.question: If we strip every render-blocking resource, first paint happens sooner. Isn't that strictly faster?
items.answer: No. For the initial render the browser needs part of the HTML plus the render-blocking CSS (and any parser-blocking scripts in the head); that is the work that makes the first paint meaningful. The goal is to keep necessary first-screen work small and make non-critical work load later, not to remove everything. Stripping all blocking CSS produces an earlier but unstyled paint, and the restyle when CSS arrives can move content and hurt LCP and CLS.
items.trap: 'First paint sooner' sounds like a universal win, so the naive move is to unblock everything. An earlier empty or unstyled paint is not meaningful progress, and the critical rendering path is precisely about the work required for a useful first render.

items.question: Both scripts are async, and app.js calls globals defined in vendor.js. What breaks?
items.answer: Execution order. async scripts download in parallel but execute as soon as each finishes downloading, with no order guarantee. If app.js is smaller or on a faster connection, it can execute before vendor.js has run and throw a ReferenceError. Dependent scripts need defer (parallel download, document order preserved, execution after parsing) or module imports, which encode the dependency explicitly. Independent scripts like analytics are the right use for async.
items.trap: async looks like a free 'make it non-blocking' upgrade applied uniformly. It silently removes the ordering guarantee that parser-blocking scripts happened to provide, so the page works locally (warm cache, fast disk) and fails intermittently in production.

items.question: Why doesn't our `type="module"` script need defer?
items.answer: Module scripts are deferred by default: they download in parallel and execute after HTML parsing completes, in document order. Adding defer to a module script is redundant, and avoiding modules because 'they block parsing' is based on classic-script behavior that does not apply.
items.trap: The naive model treats modules like classic scripts, so people either add redundant defer attributes or avoid modules fearing parser blocking. The default execution model is different, and assuming classic semantics leads to wrong loading decisions.

items.question: We added loading="lazy" to every image including the hero, the audits look cleaner, but field LCP regressed. Why?
items.answer: Lazy-loading is a deferral, not a reduction. The likely LCP image now waits until the browser considers it near the viewport before its request starts, which directly delays LCP. Keep the hero eager, discoverable in the HTML, correctly sized with responsive sources and intrinsic dimensions, and apply loading="lazy" to below-the-fold images where deferred network work is a win.
items.trap: 'Lazy means smaller and faster' applied uniformly. For the one image that feeds the LCP metric, deferral adds exactly the delay the metric measures, so a cleaner-looking audit coexists with a worse user experience.

items.question: The hero is a CSS background-image on a full-bleed section. Visually identical to an img tag, so same LCP behavior?
items.answer: No. An image referenced only in CSS is discovered after the stylesheet is fetched and parsed, so its request starts later than an image declared directly in the HTML, which the preload scanner can find immediately (https://web.dev/learn/performance/resource-hints). For a likely LCP element, make it discoverable in the HTML with an img or picture element and explicit dimensions; keep background-images for cases where the late discovery is acceptable.
items.trap: The rendered result looks the same, so the naive conclusion is that the loading behavior is the same. Discovery time differs: HTML-referenced images are found during the initial parse, CSS-referenced ones only after the CSSOM is built, which adds resource-load delay to LCP.

items.question: We preloaded our self-hosted woff2 and it downloaded twice. Why would a preload cause a duplicate download?
items.answer: Fonts are fetched in CORS mode, even when self-hosted, so the preload must carry the crossorigin attribute and match the URL the CSS actually requests. A preload without crossorigin does not match the font request the stylesheet makes, and the browser downloads the file again (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-web-fonts). The hint then wastes bandwidth instead of saving time.
items.trap: Preload feels like a pure win, so a double download looks like a browser bug. It is a request-matching failure: the hint and the real fetch must be the same request (URL and CORS mode) for the preloaded copy to be reused.

items.question: font-display: swap, is that a free win with no downside?
items.answer: No. swap shows fallback text immediately, which helps when text is the LCP element, but the swap replaces text whose metrics usually differ from the web font, so the layout can shift when the font arrives, hurting CLS. The responsible setup limits families and weights to what the page needs, uses a compressed format (woff2), matches fallback metrics as closely as practical, and reserves space where appropriate, then verifies both LCP and field CLS.
items.trap: swap is marketed as the fix for invisible text, so it reads as cost-free. It trades invisible-text delay for a potential layout shift at swap time; whether that trade is good depends on how close the fallback metrics are.

items.question: We split aggressively and the entry bundle is tiny, but the route now feels slower to open. How is a smaller bundle slower?
items.answer: Because splitting moved cost from the entry to the load path of the task. If critical UI waits on a chain of tiny chunks fetched sequentially, the user pays a request waterfall that a single bundle would not have. A smaller entry bundle is not automatically a faster task when it adds late blocking requests; compare the initial waterfall, parse and execute cost, cache behavior, and interaction delay before and after.
items.trap: Entry-bundle size is the most visible number, so it becomes the target. The user's task sits on the other side of a chunk chain, and 'smaller entry' can literally mean 'more round trips before anything is usable'.

items.question: Every route chunk bundles its own copy of the charting library. What went wrong with the splitting?
items.answer: The boundaries ignored the dependency graph. Naive per-route dynamic imports duplicate shared dependencies into each chunk, so users download the library multiple times across navigations and cache entries churn. Entry and shared-dependency splitting exist precisely to prevent duplication: extract the common library into a shared chunk that is downloaded once and cached (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/).
items.trap: 'More splitting is better' treats chunks as free. Splitting that does not account for shared dependencies increases total bytes transferred and cache churn, which is the opposite of the intended win.

items.question: Why not just preload every chunk the page might possibly need?
items.answer: A preload is for a resource needed during the current navigation, and preloaded chunks start in parallel with their parent at higher urgency, so they compete for bandwidth with the current critical work, including LCP (https://web.dev/learn/performance/resource-hints). Preloading everything turns a prioritization hint into bandwidth contention. The decision must follow an observed user path and a waterfall, and be measured against LCP and current-route bytes.
items.trap: 'Earlier is always better' assumes bandwidth is free. Preload is a prioritization decision, not an accelerator: every preloaded resource pushes against the resources the current navigation actually needs.

items.question: Prefetch and preload are basically the same hint with different spellings, right?
items.answer: No. In webpack's model a preloaded chunk starts loading in parallel with its parent and is fetched at higher urgency, because it is needed during the current navigation. A prefetched chunk waits until the parent finishes and is fetched during idle time, because it targets a likely future navigation (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/). Different scope, timing, and urgency: confusing them either delays current critical work (preload misused for future chunks) or spends idle bandwidth on the wrong resource (prefetch misused for current needs).
items.trap: The names sound interchangeable and both 'load something early', so teams pick whichever they saw in a blog post. The two hints answer different questions ('needed now' versus 'likely needed next'), and swapping them produces the failure mode of the other.

items.question: We virtualized a 200-row list to fix slow row clicks and INP did not improve. Why?
items.answer: Virtualization limits DOM size, which reduces rendering, style, and interaction work that scales with the page's DOM. It does not make each row's handler or render cheaper. If the demonstrated bottleneck was the row's own work, or something else entirely, windowing changes nothing measurable. Profile first and use virtualization when list size is the demonstrated bottleneck, not as a default upgrade for every list.
items.trap: Virtualization has a reputation as 'the list performance fix', so it gets applied without a profile. On a small list the DOM was never the bottleneck, and the team pays the complexity cost (accessibility, scroll-to-item, measurement) with no metric win.

items.question: We set overscan to 0 to keep the DOM absolutely minimal, and now fast scrolling shows blank rows. Why?
items.answer: With zero overscan, rows only render once they enter the viewport, and during fast scrolling the rendering cannot keep up with scroll velocity, so the user sees empty space until rows catch up. Overscan exists to render rows slightly beyond the viewport and cover that gap; too much overscan gives back the DOM work you were avoiding, so it is a tuning trade-off, not a maximization.
items.trap: Minimizing the DOM at all costs treats overscan as pure overhead. Overscan is the buffer that makes windowing survive fast scrolls; setting it to zero optimizes a number (DOM nodes) at the cost of the experience (visible blank flashes).

items.question: CI Lighthouse says 98 but CrUX says the mobile segment fails LCP. Which number is the truth?
items.answer: Both are true for what they measure. Lighthouse is a controlled run with a chosen device, network, location, cache state, and scripted behavior; CrUX is a distribution from real devices, networks, locations, and cache states. The lab run can pass while the field population fails because they are different populations and scenarios. Use the field data to prioritize user impact and segment the affected population, and use lab traces to reproduce and isolate the cause before shipping.
items.trap: The question frames them as competing measurements of the same thing, inviting 'one of them is wrong'. They answer different questions; the field distribution governs what users experience, and the lab explains why.

items.question: We shipped the LCP fix today and CrUX still shows failure a week later. Did the fix not work?
items.answer: You cannot tell yet. CrUX data is a 28-day rolling average of aggregated field experiences (https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux/api), so a fix shipped this week is diluted by up to four weeks of pre-fix data. Verify sooner with your own RUM at the 75th percentile for the affected route and device segment, and let CrUX converge over its window before judging.
items.trap: Treating CrUX like a live dashboard. The rolling aggregation means same-day or same-week movement is impossible by construction; the naive conclusion 'the fix failed, revert it' acts on a number that structurally cannot have moved yet.

items.question: We report vitals in the unload handler. Why are we losing a large share of samples?
items.answer: Because unload is not reliable for every lifecycle: mobile users frequently background the page or close the tab without an unload event firing, and lifecycle behavior differs across browsers. Send the data when the page becomes hidden (visibilitychange to hidden) as well as on unload, so a sample is captured the first time the page leaves the viewport.
items.trap: unload feels like the natural 'page is done' hook, and on desktop testing it usually fires, so the loss is invisible to the developers who built it. The missing samples skew toward exactly the mobile populations that most need monitoring.

items.question: We sum every layout-shift entry's value as our CLS, and our number is far higher than CrUX. Why?
items.answer: Because CLS is not a raw sum. The metric aggregates shifts into session windows and reports the largest window score, so many small unrelated shifts over a long visit do not simply add up (https://web.dev/articles/cls). Hand-rolled arithmetic also drifts on edge cases the reference implementation handles. Use the web-vitals library's onCLS, which implements the metric's defined aggregation rules, instead of recomputing the metric from raw entries.
items.trap: 'CLS equals the sum of shift scores' is the obvious interpretation of the entries. The metric spec defines a session-window aggregation precisely so that long sessions are not punished linearly; a raw sum both overstates long visits and can understate the worst burst.

items.question: Why is a single global budget, say 300KB of JavaScript for the whole site, the wrong shape?
items.answer: Because it is not tied to any route, device class, or user task. A marketing landing page and a data-heavy dashboard have different legitimate needs: the global cap either blocks necessary work on heavy routes or excuses waste on light ones. Tie budgets to a route and device class, combine quantity budgets (initial JavaScript, image bytes, request count, third-party cost) with user-centric budgets (LCP, INP, CLS), and set them from a measured baseline.
items.trap: One global number is easy to communicate and enforce, which makes it attractive. But a budget that ignores the user task regulates the wrong thing: teams hit the number by shifting cost around it (late chunks, more requests) rather than by improving the task.

items.question: Every PR passes the CI budget checks, yet the field distribution regressed after release. How is that possible?
items.answer: CI enforces repeatable lab signals on a controlled scenario. A passing synthetic budget can still hide a real-user regression: different devices, networks, cache states, third-party behavior, or interactions the lab never performs. That is why budgets need field monitoring after release, comparing the same route and segment, with alerts against a baseline.
items.trap: Green CI reads as 'performance is protected'. The budget verified the scenario it runs; real users run different scenarios, so the regression the budget cannot see still ships.

items.question: You profiled on your development machine and found no long tasks, but users report jank. What is wrong with the trace?
items.answer: The scenario, not the finding. A trace is evidence about the scenario you recorded: a fast dev machine with a warm cache hides main-thread costs that real devices pay. Reproduce with a representative device and throttled CPU matching the affected field segment, then re-record. If users on low-end mobile report the jank, throttle to that class of device before concluding anything.
items.trap: 'No bottleneck in my trace' gets generalized to 'no bottleneck'. The trace is only as representative as the device, network, and cache state it was captured under.

items.question: The trace showed one long task, we fixed it, users still complain. Why?
items.answer: Because a profile is evidence about one scenario, not proof that every user has the same bottleneck. Different routes, devices, and interactions can have different causes. Change one cause at a time, record again, compare both the trace evidence and the user-facing metric, and check field data for the affected segment to confirm the fix moved the number real users experience.
items.trap: A single confirming trace feels like a diagnosis of the population. It is a diagnosis of one recorded scenario; shipping the fix and moving on skips the verification loop that would have caught the second bottleneck.

items.question: Nothing visually changed between frames, yet the trace shows Recalculate Style and Layout right before our getBoundingClientRect call every frame. Why is the browser recalculating layout it already computed?
items.answer: Because something wrote first. A style or DOM write earlier in the same frame invalidated the cached layout, so the geometry read cannot be answered from the previous layout and forces a recalculation. That is the forced-layout cost: it is not the read itself but the read landing after a write. Batch the reads before the writes, or cache the measurement, so the frame's geometry is queried once.
items.trap: The intuition is 'reads are cheap if nothing changed'. After a write, layout is dirty by definition, and the read pays for the recalculation; the trace shows the cost attached to the read, which misattributes the cause to the read instead of the interleaving.

items.question: Should we ban all geometry reads like getBoundingClientRect to be safe?
items.answer: No. The goal is not to ban reads; it is to avoid forcing the browser to recalculate the same layout repeatedly within a frame. Batch reads before writes, calculate from cached measurements where possible, avoid querying layout inside large loops, and prefer transforms for movement. A single batched read per frame is fine and often necessary.
items.trap: Hearing 'reads cause thrashing' invites overcorrection to zero reads. The cost comes from the read-write interleaving pattern, not from reads existing; banning them produces contorted code for no measurable win.

items.question: Why not have the platform team own every resource hint centrally? Wouldn't that stop teams from misusing them?
items.answer: Centralizing hints without route context is as risky as letting every team add them. A preload must be required during the current navigation and a prefetch must represent a credible future path, and those are route-level judgments a central owner cannot make reliably. The workable split is centralized policy (a small set of allowed use cases, review on route changes, tracking hint count, duplicate downloads, LCP, and route-transition latency) with route teams accountable for their user task.
items.trap: 'Central control equals safety' assumes the failure is lack of ownership. The failure is usually lack of route context: a hint that was correct for one navigation pattern becomes stale or harmful when the route changes, regardless of who owns it.

items.question: Every repo enforces budgets in CI and they are all green. Isn't performance now a durable property?
items.answer: Green CI is necessary but not sufficient. Durable performance is decided by production percentiles: whether users on real devices improved. Without a regression process that links a release, route, segment, and metric to an owner or rollback, drift accumulates invisibly, especially from third-party scripts and design-system changes, because shared dependencies affect every route at once.
items.trap: CI green reads as a solved property because it is the most visible signal. CI verifies lab scenarios on each PR; it does not observe the field distribution, so slow drift from third parties or the design system passes every check while users get slower.

items.question: Our PerformanceObserver registers for an entry type but reports nothing for some pageviews even though the entries exist. Why?
items.answer: Because entries may have been recorded before the observer was created. observe() only delivers entries that happen after registration unless you opt into buffered observation, which replays already-recorded entries of that type. Register with buffered: true when the events of interest (long tasks, shifts, paints) may predate your script's execution.
items.trap: The assumption is that observe() streams the full history of the entry type. Without buffered: true it is a live tap, not a log: anything before registration is invisible, which silently biases the sample toward late pageviews.

items.question: Why not hand-roll the Core Web Vitals from raw PerformanceObserver entries and skip the library?
items.answer: Because the API is an input to a reporting design, not the metric itself. CLS needs its defined aggregation rules rather than a raw sum; INP has its own selection semantics across interactions; entries can arrive before observers exist (buffering); iframe content may be inaccessible to the top-level page; and unload is not a reliable reporting moment. A maintained reference implementation like web-vitals exists precisely to encode those rules, so prefer it and spend your effort on adding route and release context and reporting at visibility changes.
items.trap: 'The API emits the entries, so the metric is a reduce away.' The metric semantics live in aggregation and lifecycle rules the raw entries do not carry, and hand-rolled versions diverge from CrUX in ways that are hard to notice until the numbers disagree.

mcqs.question: Your team wants a defensible pass/fail answer for Core Web Vitals. What is the correct basis for that decision?
options: A single Lighthouse run against the production URL on the desktop preset
The 75th percentile of field data for each metric, assessed per metric and segmented by mobile and desktop
The average of LCP, INP, and CLS values collected in RUM, reported as one score
The median FID from the most recent CrUX period
mcqs.explanation: Core Web Vitals pass/fail is a field-data question: each metric is assessed on its distribution at the 75th percentile, and mobile and desktop are segmented rather than blended (https://web.dev/articles/vitals). The single Lighthouse run is the strongest distractor because Lighthouse is genuinely useful, but it is one controlled lab run, not a substitute for what real users experienced. Averaging hides the tail that the p75 exists to expose, and blending three metrics into one score has no meaning in the assessment. The FID option reaches for a metric that was replaced by INP as the responsiveness vital (https://web.dev/articles/inp), and a median is the wrong statistic anyway.

mcqs.question: Field data shows poor LCP on a product page. The LCP element is a text block rendered on the client after hydration. Which fix most directly targets the dominant phase?
options: Convert the hero image to AVIF and cut its bytes by 70%
Preload the hero image so it arrives earlier
Reduce render delay: serve the content server-rendered and remove render-blocking work so the text paints earlier
Add loading="lazy" to below-the-fold images
mcqs.explanation: LCP time is the sum of TTFB, resource-load delay, resource-load duration, and render delay (https://web.dev/articles/lcp). When the LCP element is text that only appears after client-side rendering or hydration, the dominant phase is render delay, so server-rendering the content and reducing render-blocking work attacks the measured problem. Image compression is the strongest distractor because it is the reflex LCP fix, but the LCP element is not an image, so its bytes are irrelevant here. Preloading the hero image optimizes a resource that is not the LCP element, and lazy-loading below-the-fold images helps offscreen network work but does nothing for when the largest text block first renders.

mcqs.question: A page loads two classic scripts in the head: vendor.js (large, no dependencies) and app.js (depends on vendor.js). Order matters and both are needed to initialize the UI. What is the correct loading setup?
options: Both async: downloads run in parallel and execution order does not matter
app.js defer, vendor.js async: the small one waits, the big one does not
Both defer: downloads run in parallel, document order is preserved, and both run after parsing
Leave both without attributes: parser-blocking guarantees correctness, so it is the safest choice
mcqs.explanation: defer downloads both scripts in parallel, preserves document order, and executes after HTML parsing, which satisfies both the dependency and the ordering requirement while removing parser blocking. The both-async option is the strongest distractor because async also parallelizes downloads, but async executes each script as soon as it is ready with no order guarantee, so app.js can run before vendor.js and throw. The mixed defer/async setup still allows app.js to execute before vendor.js has run. Leaving both parser-blocking is correct but slow: classic scripts without attributes serialize fetch and execution and stall DOM construction. Module scripts are an alternative since they are deferred by default and can encode the dependency with an import.

mcqs.question: Which loading setup best serves a product page with a large hero image (the likely LCP element) and a grid of below-the-fold related-product images?
options: loading="lazy" on every image including the hero, to minimize initial network work
Hero as a CSS background-image so it does not block parsing; grid images eager
Every image eager but heavily compressed, so nothing is ever deferred
Hero eager with intrinsic dimensions and responsive sources; grid images loading="lazy" with dimensions
mcqs.explanation: The likely LCP image must be eager, discoverable in the HTML, sized with responsive sources, and carry intrinsic dimensions, while below-the-fold images are the correct target for loading="lazy" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Performance/Guides/Lazy_loading). The lazy-everything option is the strongest distractor because it looks like a clean audit win, but deferring the LCP image delays the very metric it feeds. The CSS background-image option trades a real problem for a worse one: a background image is discovered only after the stylesheet is fetched and parsed, adding resource-load delay to the likely LCP (https://web.dev/learn/performance/resource-hints). The all-eager option wastes mobile bandwidth by sending desktop-sized bytes and forgoes deferral where it is free.

mcqs.question: A team preloads their self-hosted critical font with `<link rel="preload" href="/app-sans.woff2" as="font">`. The waterfall shows the font downloading twice. Why?
options: Preload does not work for font files; only scripts and stylesheets can be preloaded
The preload is missing crossorigin: fonts are fetched in CORS mode even when self-hosted, so the hinted request does not match the CSS's request and the browser downloads the font again
woff2 cannot be preloaded; the team should switch to woff
The font file must be base64-inlined into the CSS to avoid a second download
mcqs.explanation: Fonts are CORS resources, so a font preload must include crossorigin and match the URL the stylesheet requests; otherwise the preload is not reused and the font is fetched twice (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-web-fonts). The 'preload does not work for fonts' option is the strongest distractor because it sounds like a plausible hint limitation, but fonts are one of the most common and recommended preload use cases. The woff2 option invents a format restriction that does not exist; woff2 is the recommended web font format. Base64-inlining the font would avoid the second request by making the CSS enormous, which delays other critical work.

mcqs.question: After aggressive per-route splitting, initial JavaScript dropped to 60KB, but opening the settings route now feels slower than before the split. What is the most likely cause?
options: The settings UI waits on a chain of small chunks fetched sequentially, and shared dependencies may be duplicated across them
Modern browsers cannot cache small chunks efficiently, so every navigation re-downloads them
Dynamic import() is inherently slower than a static import at runtime
The entry bundle is still too large for the route to initialize
mcqs.explanation: Splitting is harmful when critical UI waits on a chain of tiny chunks or when shared dependencies are duplicated: a smaller entry bundle is not automatically a faster task if it adds late blocking requests (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/). The 'entry bundle is still too large' option is the strongest distractor because entry size is the number everyone watches, but the premise says it dropped to 60KB; the cost moved to the route's load path. The browser-caching option misattributes the problem to caching, which handles small chunks fine when cache headers are correct. The import() option blames the import mechanism, which is cheap; the cost is the extra round trips and duplicated code the boundaries created.

mcqs.question: Analytics shows users of the dashboard route almost always visit the settings route next. The team wants the settings chunk available for that next navigation without competing with the current route's critical resources. Which approach fits?
options: Preload the settings chunk: it starts in parallel with the current chunk at higher urgency
Inline the settings chunk into the entry bundle so it is always present
Prefetch the settings chunk: it is fetched after the parent chunk finishes, during idle time
Do nothing and fetch the chunk on click: the network is fast enough
mcqs.explanation: A prefetch targets a credible future navigation: in webpack's model the prefetched chunk waits until the parent finishes and is fetched during idle time, so it does not compete with the current navigation's critical work (https://webpack.js.org/guides/code-splitting/). The preload option is the strongest distractor because preload also fetches early, but preload is for resources needed during the current navigation and runs at higher urgency in parallel with the parent, which is exactly the bandwidth competition the team wants to avoid. Inlining into the entry bloats every dashboard visit with code that other routes never need. Fetching on click forfeits the observed user path and pays the chunk latency on every transition.

mcqs.question: A team virtualizes a 200-item list to improve INP on row clicks, but field INP is unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The list needs more overscan to cover the interaction window
Virtualization limits DOM size but does not make each row's handler or render work cheaper; the bottleneck was likely elsewhere
The virtualization library itself is the bottleneck; switching libraries will fix it
INP only measures the first interaction on the page, and that one was already fast
mcqs.explanation: Virtualization reduces rendering, style, and interaction work that scales with DOM size, but it does not make each row cheaper; if the demonstrated bottleneck is the row's own handler or something else entirely, windowing moves nothing (https://web.dev/articles/dom-size-and-interactivity). Profile before virtualizing and use it when list size is the demonstrated bottleneck. The 'INP only measures the first interaction' option is the strongest distractor because it reaches for a real-sounding metric fact, but it describes FID, which only measured the first interaction's input delay; INP observes interactions across the page lifetime (https://web.dev/articles/inp). The overscan option tunes a scroll-smoothing parameter that has nothing to do with click latency. The library option blames the tool before establishing that DOM size was ever the problem.

mcqs.question: Lighthouse in CI reports 95+ for a route, but CrUX shows the mobile segment failing LCP. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Use the field data to confirm the affected segment, then reproduce with a throttled, mobile-like lab trace to isolate the cause
Trust Lighthouse: CrUX is noisy field data and the lab run is controlled
Trust CrUX alone and roll back the last release that touched the route
Run Lighthouse five more times and report the best score
mcqs.explanation: Lab and field answer different questions: field data identifies the affected population and prioritizes user impact, and lab traces reproduce and isolate the cause under controlled conditions (https://web.dev/articles/lab-and-field-data-differences). The 'trust Lighthouse' option is the strongest distractor because 'controlled' sounds like 'more trustworthy', but the lab's device, network, and cache choices may simply not match the failing mobile population. Rolling back on CrUX alone acts on field data without a diagnosis and reverts code that may not be the cause. Repeated Lighthouse runs are cherry-picking: they still measure the same unrepresentative scenario.

mcqs.question: A loop updates 500 rows by reading row.getBoundingClientRect().height and then writing row.style.top and row.style.left, one row at a time. The interaction is janky. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: Wrap each iteration in requestAnimationFrame so the browser batches it
Hoist all geometry reads before all writes: collect the measurements first, then apply the position changes in a second pass
Replace the transform-based approach with top and left so the browser avoids transform math
Move the loop into a web worker so it runs off the main thread
mcqs.explanation: The loop interleaves layout reads with style writes: after each write the layout is dirty, so the next read forces a Recalculate Style and Layout pass, 500 times per interaction. Batching all reads before all writes collapses that to one layout (https://web.dev/articles/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing). The requestAnimationFrame option is the strongest distractor because rAF sounds like a batching primitive, but it only schedules when the callback runs; the read-write interleaving inside the callback thrashes exactly the same. The top/left option makes things worse: writing top and left triggers layout on every write, while transforms avoid it. The worker option is impossible: DOM APIs do not exist in workers.

mcqs.question: Which performance-budget design is most likely to actually change what teams build?
options: A single global JavaScript byte cap for the whole site, reviewed in a monthly report
A Lighthouse performance-score floor of 90 enforced in CI
Budgets owned and applied identically by the platform team across every route

Route- and device-class-specific budgets combining quantity caps (JS and image bytes, request count, third-party cost) with user-centric metrics (LCP, INP, CLS), enforced in CI and monitored in field, where every exception carries an owner, expiry, and reason
mcqs.explanation: Budgets that change behavior are tied to a route, device class, and user task; they combine quantity budgets with user-centric metrics, are set from a measured baseline, are enforced in CI for repeatable lab signals, and are monitored in field distributions after release, because a passing synthetic budget can still hide a real-user regression (https://web.dev/articles/performance-budgets-101). The global byte cap is the strongest distractor because it is easy to communicate, but it is not tied to any user task, so it either blocks necessary routes or excuses wasteful ones. The score floor proxies everything through one lab number. Identical platform-owned budgets ignore route context, the same failure mode as centralizing resource hints without it.

scenarios.prompt: This reorder animation runs at roughly 12fps on mid-range phones, and a Performance trace shows one long task with repeated Recalculate Style and Layout entries. Diagnose the root cause and rewrite the function so the interaction stays smooth. Explain what the trace should look like after the fix.
rubric: Identifies forced layout: the read-after-write interleaving forces Recalculate Style and Layout per row, not once per frame
Batches all geometry reads before all writes instead of reaching for rAF or debounce wrappers
Replaces top/left with transform so movement no longer triggers layout
Mentions caching measurements or reducing the affected DOM for repeated interactions
Verifies the fix by re-recording the same trace scenario and comparing the user-facing metric

scenarios.prompt: Predict what happens at runtime with this document, explain the failure mode and when it occurs, then rewrite the script loading so the page initializes reliably without blocking parsing more than necessary.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Prediction: analytics.js is a classic script with no attribute, so it blocks HTML parsing while it is fetched and executed, delaying DOM construction for a script that has no dependency on the document. vendor.js and app.js are async: they download in parallel, but each executes as soon as it has downloaded, with no order guarantee. app.js is smaller than vendor.js, so on a cold cache it frequently finishes first, executes, and calls window.Vendor.render before vendor.js has run, throwing a ReferenceError and leaving the page blank. The failure is intermittent by construction: with a warm cache, or when vendor.js happens to win the race, the page works, which is why it survives testing. Fix: analytics.js is independent, so it should be async. vendor.js and app.js have a dependency and an ordering requirement, so both should be defer: parallel download, document order preserved, execution after parsing. An even better shape is modules, which are deferred by default and encode the dependency explicitly:

```html
<script async src="/analytics.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="/app.js"></script>
```

with app.js importing vendor. Then confirm the actual request and execution order in the Network and Performance panels rather than trusting the attributes.
rubric: Predicts the ReferenceError: async does not preserve execution order, so app.js can execute before vendor.js
Explains why the bug is intermittent (cache and network races), which is why it survives testing
Identifies analytics.js as parser-blocking and makes it async since it is independent
Uses defer, or modules with an explicit import, for the dependent pair so order is preserved without blocking parsing
Verifies the final request and execution order in the Network and Performance panels

scenarios.prompt: This field-vitals instrumentation shipped to production. The team's dashboard disagrees with CrUX, and a large share of pageviews never reports anything. Identify at least three distinct problems with the measurement design and rewrite the snippet.
rubric: Recognizes CLS is not a raw sum and replaces the hand-rolled math with onCLS and its defined aggregation rules
Moves reporting to visibilitychange (page hidden) in addition to unload, explaining why unload loses samples
Adds route, release, and device context so regressions can be segmented and acted on
Spots the missing buffered observation for entries recorded before the observer existed
Keeps the reference implementation as the source of metric semantics instead of reimplementing them

scenarios.prompt: After a redesign, this product page regressed LCP and CLS in field data, worst on mobile. Audit the loading strategy in the component, explain each problem and which metric it hurts, and refactor it.
